requests.discriminates: EquateStringCaseInsensitive is Go simple folding (strings.EqualFold), not JavaScript casing and not byte equality: it accepts s/ſ and k/K, rejects i/İ and i/ı that a JS or Turkish casing would join, and decodes every malformed byte as one U+FFFD, so \xff folds equal to \xfe and to the encoded replacement character.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: ToLowerJS is String.prototype.toLowerCase, not Go simple lowering: Final_Sigma context turns the trailing sigma of ΑΣ into ς while ΑΣΒ keeps σ, a following Case_Ignorable code point ('.' or U+0301) is skipped rather than counted as a following cased letter, so ΑΣ. and ΑΣ́ still end in ς, and İ expands to i plus U+0307. A lone-surrogate sentinel survives byte for byte while a malformed byte is repaired to U+FFFD, so the two byte classes must not be conflated.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: ToUpperJS is a full case mapping: ß becomes the two characters SS and ﬁ becomes FI, which Go's simple unicode.ToUpper does not do, and ı uppercases to I while U+1E9E is already upper. Both final and medial sigma map to Σ, so the Final_Sigma context that ToLowerJS tracks has no upper counterpart. Lone surrogates are copied verbatim.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: LowerFirstChar uses plain UTF-8 decoding and Go simple lowering, so it differs from ToLowerJS on exactly the inputs that matter: İ becomes i with no combining dot, ΑΣ lowers only the first rune, and a malformed or lone-surrogate leading byte is consumed one byte at a time and replaced by the three bytes of U+FFFD, growing the string. The empty string returns unchanged because DecodeRuneInString reports width zero.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The early return compares the BYTE length against a RUNE budget, so 'abc' with 4 returns early while 'ééé' with 2 truncates and 'é' with 1 returns whole. A non-positive budget yields the empty string even for empty input, and each malformed byte counts as one rune, so \xff\xffab with 3 keeps three bytes.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The sentinel window is ED A0..BF 80..BF, so ED 9F BF still decodes as ordinary UTF-8 (U+D7FF) while ED A0 80 decodes as U+D800 with width 3, and a truncated or out-of-window sequence falls back to utf8.DecodeRuneInString's one-byte RuneError. Encoding a non-surrogate above U+10FFFF yields U+FFFD, and an ill-formed surrogate pair yields RuneError instead of a computed code point.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The fast path keys on the byte 0xED alone, so a plain U+D7FF (ED 9F BF) and a bare 0xED take the slow path and must come back unchanged. Only an adjacent high-then-low sentinel pair merges: a low followed by a high, a high followed by a letter and an unpaired half are all preserved, so a caller cannot rely on the output being valid UTF-8.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: Three contracts over one corpus. Byte comparison keeps \xff above \xfe, while CompareStringsCaseInsensitive decodes runes first and calls them equal because both are RuneError - and equal again against the encoded U+FFFD even though the byte lengths differ. It lowercases per rune rather than folding, so s/ſ stay unequal although EqualFold accepts them; á and á stay unequal because nothing normalises. The then-sensitive comparer breaks the a/A tie by bytes, and the two selector functions must return exactly those implementations.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: Correction to an earlier survey: at this pin BOTH case-insensitive comparers lowercase. CompareStringsCaseInsensitive calls unicode.ToLower per rune and the eslint-compatible one calls strings.ToLower, and only the stale doc comment still says uppercase. Seven of the nine pairs invert under an uppercasing implementation, because '_' (0x5F), '[' (0x5B), '^' (0x5E) and '`' (0x60) sit between the ASCII upper and lower letter blocks - the range 91-96 the doc comment names. The last two are the boundary controls that do not invert: '{' (0x7B) sits above both blocks and so stays above every letter either way, and 'Z' vs 'a' answers 1 under both foldings, separating the two case-insensitive comparers from the byte comparer, which answers -1.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The case-insensitive path folds a BYTE window cut to the affix's byte length, so it can slice a rune in half: 'İx' with prefix 'i' compares one byte and is false, and 'straße' with suffix 'SSE' is false because EqualFold is simple folding, not full case folding. The length guard is checked before slicing, and HasPrefixAndSuffixWithoutOverlap rejects 'a' with prefix 'a' and suffix 'a' although each matches on its own.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: These are the raw generated ID_Start / ID_Continue tables, not the scanner's identifier predicate: '$' is in neither, while '_' and ZWNJ/ZWJ (U+200C-U+200D, which the generated part table carries explicitly) are Continue but not Start, so any implementation that reuses the scanner's start set, which adds '$' and '_' itself, disagrees here. Surrogates, U+FFFD, a code point above U+10FFFF and a negative rune must all answer false rather than panicking or indexing out of range.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The whitespace set is the ECMAScript table, not unicode.IsSpace and not unicode.Zs: U+0085 and U+200B count as single-line whitespace here while U+180E does not, and only LF, CR, U+2028 and U+2029 are line breaks, so U+0085 is whitespace without being a break. The digit and letter predicates are ASCII-only, so U+0660 and U+FF10 are not digits and '_' is not a letter.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: EncodeURI walks BYTES, so every byte outside the unreserved set becomes one uppercase %XX pair: a malformed 0xFF becomes %FF rather than the three escapes of U+FFFD, and a multi-byte rune becomes one escape per byte. The set that is left alone is the ECMAScript one, which keeps ; / ? : @ & = + $ , # - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) and escapes %, [, ], { and }.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The length probe recognises UTF-16 BOMs the rest of the compiler cannot decode, so RemoveByteOrderMark strips two bytes from FE FF and leaves invalid UTF-8 behind, and AddUTF8ByteOrderMark refuses to prepend one whenever any BOM is already present - including a UTF-16 one it is not converting. A bare FE or FF, or an incomplete EF BB, is not a BOM, so the UTF-8 mark is prepended in front of it.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: SplitLines is a byte scanner: CRLF is one break, a lone CR is a break, U+2028 is not, and a trailing break never produces a final empty line - so 'a\n' has one line and '\n' has one empty line. GuessIndentation measures leading whitespace in BYTES using the rune-level whitespace set, so one NBSP contributes two and U+2028 three, while U+180E is not whitespace at all; empty lines are skipped, and an all-empty or empty input returns 0 rather than the MAX_SMI sentinel.
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: StripQuotes compares the first and last RUNES and strips only ' " or `, so a two-byte \xff\xff whose halves both decode to RuneError is left alone, and a string shorter than two bytes is returned as is. UnquoteString's `\\.` replacement drops the backslash before any rune except LF, because Go's '.' excludes it: a backslash before a real newline survives while one before CR does not. It is not a real unescape, so \n stays the letter n. The backslash inputs reach the replacement the quoted form performs: the pinned code replaces every backslash-something pair with the something, faithfully reproducing the original regular expression rather than unescaping, so a quoted backslash-n becomes the letter n and not a line feed, a doubled backslash becomes one, and an escaped quote becomes a bare quote. A port that called a real unquote would differ on every one of them. The unquoted input with a backslash shows that the replacement runs on whatever StripQuotes returned, quoted or not. The backslash-newline inputs separate the replacement from a naive unescape in the other direction: the pinned pattern is the regular expression \\. and Go's dot does not match a line feed by default, so a backslash immediately before a newline is left in place where every other backslash is removed
requests.subject: stringutil

requests.discriminates: The outer regexp allows a bare major or major.minor and defaults the rest to zero, but rejects a leading zero, a fourth component, a 'v' prefix and any surrounding space. A prerelease is then re-validated, so 1.2.3-01 fails while the same text is a legal RANGE operand. Because the regexp is (?i), RE2 folds [a-z] onto U+017F and U+212A, which are therefore legal prerelease identifiers. Overflow is the sharpest case: the numeric component keeps strconv's saturated 4294967295 and the partially filled Version is returned beside the strconv range error, so both the value and the error text are frozen.
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: Each pair is compared in both directions, so an asymmetric comparator is caught. Build metadata never participates, a prerelease sorts below its release, a numeric identifier sorts below an alphanumeric one, and a shorter identifier list sorts first. The two overflow pairs pin the documented fallback: when a numeric identifier exceeds uint32 the comparison falls back to identifier LENGTH, and to plain ASCII order when the lengths are equal. A nil version sorts below every parsed version and equal to another nil.
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: The caret's upper bound depends on which component is the first non-zero one AND on which component was a wildcard, which is where hand-ported range code usually goes wrong: ^0.0.3 stops at 0.0.4, ^0.2.3 at 0.3.0 and ^1.2.3 at 2.0.0, while ^0.0 and ^0.0.x stop at 0.1.0 because the patch wildcard promotes the bound. The tilde's upper bound always increments the minor, or the major when the minor is a wildcard, so ~0.0.3 stops at 0.1.0 where ^0.0.3 stops at 0.0.4. ~1.2 and ~1.2.3 share the upper bound <1.3.0 but not the lower one: a missing patch defaults to 0 and the tilde branch gives its >= comparator no prerelease floor, so ~1.2 is >=1.2.0 and admits 1.2.3-alpha while ~1.2.3 is >=1.2.3 and rejects it. ~1 widens to >=1.0.0 <2.0.0. Every bound is also probed by membership, so a correct rendering with wrong comparators still fails.
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: Range boundaries were entirely missing from the earlier survey. A wildcard major erases the whole comparator unless the operator is < or >, and then BOTH become '<0.0.0-0', so '>*' matches nothing rather than everything. An empty range, '||' and '~*' all render as '*' and accept every version. A wildcard minor or patch injects the '-0' prerelease floor, which is what makes '1.x' exclude 2.0.0-0. Whitespace is split with the regexp's ASCII \s before each token is matched, so '>= 1.2.3' is INVALID while a trailing vertical tab is trimmed by strings.TrimSpace and '1.2.3\v' is valid. A range operand skips the stricter identifier check, so '1.2.3-01' parses here although it fails TryParseVersion.
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: Test is a plain disjunction of conjunctions over Version.Compare, with no npm-style 'prereleases only match their own tuple' rule: >=1.2.3-alpha admits 1.2.3-beta and every later release, and 1.x admits 1.0.0-0 because of the injected floor while excluding 2.0.0-0. An empty disjunction accepts everything, including a nil version, while '<*' accepts ONLY a nil version, because nil sorts below 0.0.0-0.
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: Number.String is Number.prototype.toString, not Go's %v: NaN, Infinity and -Infinity are spelled out, negative zero renders as '0' because the safe-integer fast path compares float64(0) to -0.0 and wins, and the exponent switch sits at 1e21 and 1e-6 - 1e20 prints in full, 1e21 prints as 1e+21 and 1e-7 prints as 1e-7 with the two-digit exponent already trimmed. The subnormal 5e-324 and 0.1+0.2 pin shortest round-trip formatting.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: StringToNumber, not strconv: an empty or all-whitespace string is 0 and only the ECMAScript whitespace set is trimmed (so U+FEFF and U+000B are, U+0085 is not), 'Infinity' is accepted but 'infinity' is not, radix prefixes are accepted only unsigned so '-0x10' is NaN, leading zeros never mean octal, a separator is never allowed, and overflow saturates to Infinity while underflow returns +0 because strconv's range error carries a usable value. '-0' must come back as negative zero, which is why every result carries its bit pattern; a NaN reports the category instead, because ECMAScript has one NaN and Go's runtime payload is not a contract.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: ToInt32 wraps modulo 2^32 instead of saturating, which is the opposite of a plain Rust `as i32` cast: 4294967295 is -1, 2147483648 is i32::MIN and 4294967296 is 0. Non-finite values and both zeros are 0, fractions truncate toward zero before the reduction, and ToUint32 is only a reinterpretation of the same bits, so the two must never disagree about which value they reduced.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: The shift count is ToUint32 masked with 31, so shifting by 32 is a no-op and shifting by 33 shifts one; a NaN or negative count is reduced the same way rather than panicking, which a Rust `<<` would do. The unsigned right shift is the only operator whose result leaves the int32 range, so -1 >>> 0 must be 4294967295 and not -1. Every operand is reduced to int32 first, so 2147483648 | 1 is -2147483647, and the count is masked rather than clamped, which is why 1 << 63 is i32::MIN rather than zero.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: Remainder is the JavaScript % operator, not math.Mod alone: an infinite dividend or a zero divisor is NaN, an infinite divisor returns the dividend unchanged, and a zero dividend keeps its sign, so -0 % 5 is negative zero. Exponentiate special-cases +-1 to an infinite exponent and 1 to NaN, both of which ordinary powf gets wrong, and it routes integer base/exponent pairs whose result exceeds 53 bits through exact big-integer arithmetic rounded at 256 bits, so 3**34 and 10**21 must match that path and not powf. Results carry bit patterns; a NaN reports only its category, because its payload is not observable.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: IsInf ignores the sign, so both infinities report true, and isNonFinite answers the same question with one exponent-mask test - a single predicate that must agree with IsNaN or IsInf on every input including a NaN payload. Floor and trunc part company below zero (-0.5 floors to -1 and truncates to -0) and Abs(-0) is +0, so the results carry bit patterns, with a NaN reporting only its category because its payload is not observable. toShiftCount is the masked count the shift operators are built on, recorded directly rather than inferred from a shift result.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: The radix branch is selected by the SECOND BYTE alone, so '1_000n' takes the decimal path and keeps its separator verbatim while '0b_101n' goes through big.Int and becomes 5; a one-character input can never take the radix path. Only one trailing 'n' is stripped, so '0n0' is not a literal at all and comes back as 'n0'. An all-zero magnitude normalises to the single digit 0, and NewPseudoBigInt stores zero as the EMPTY string and refuses to mark it negative, which is the representation every consumer compares against. A leading '-' shifts the byte the radix switch reads, so '-0x10n' takes the decimal path too and comes back as the literal '-0x10', and that path copies BYTES rather than text, so the malformed 0xFF of '1\xff0n' survives it - which is why every result here is reported as hex rather than as a JSON string that encoding/json and from_utf8_lossy would both repair to U+FFFD.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: ParseValidBigInt splits the sign BEFORE the radix parse, which is the only way '-0x10n' becomes -16: the radix branch never accepts a sign itself. The sign is then dropped again for any zero magnitude, so '-0n' and '-000n' are indistinguishable from '0n'. Sign is the predicate the checker branches on and must agree with that normalisation rather than with the negative flag it was constructed with.
requests.subject: jsnum

requests.discriminates: the increment helpers build a fresh version from the incremented component alone, so the upper bound a caret or tilde range derives carries no prerelease and no build: the operand's own prerelease survives in the lower bound while the upper bound is a bare release. A port that copied the operand and bumped one field would keep them, and the rendered range would differ even where the membership answers happened to agree, which is why the rendered form is compared and not only the tests
requests.subject: semver

requests.discriminates: a range that fails to parse is still returned, carrying no alternatives, and an empty disjunction is specified to admit every version, so a failed parse yields a range that matches everything rather than nothing; a port that returned an error and defaulted to no match would invert every answer here. The rendered form is the wildcard for the same reason: the disjunction writes it when it emitted no bytes of its own
requests.subject: semver
